claims.text: VZrHfNbTa is the high-entropy alloy substrate considered in the hypothesis.
The initial VZrHfNbTa alloy is nanostructured and has a uniform phase distribution.
During high-temperature sintering, zirconium from VZrHfNbTa diffuses into an applied hafnium coating.
Zirconium diffusion into the hafnium coating forms an HfZr transition layer.
The HfZr transition layer is an intermetallic phase.
The HfZr transition layer chemically bonds the hafnium coating to the HEA substrate.
The HfZr transition layer acts as a physical diffusion barrier.
The HfZr transition layer modifies surface reactivity.
The modified surface reactivity favors formation of a dense, protective HfO2 scale.
The transition layer and protective HfO2 scale suppress internal oxidation and oxidation penetration.
Suppression of oxidation penetration mitigates structural degradation of the nanoalloy.
The diffusion-induced HfZr transition layer governs both structural and chemical stability at high temperature.
After oxidation in air at approximately 1600 °C for 5 hours, the hafnium-coated sample will gain less weight than the uncoated HEA.
After oxidation in air at approximately 1600 °C for 5 hours, the hafnium-coated sample will exhibit less oxide penetration than the uncoated HEA.
After oxidation in air at approximately 1600 °C for 5 hours, the hafnium-coated sample will retain greater structural integrity than the uncoated HEA.
Uncoated HEA samples are expected to undergo extensive internal oxidation and microstructural deterioration under the specified oxidation conditions.
The prediction applies to nanoscale HEA structures oxidized in air near 1600 °C for about 5 hours.
Substantially different temperatures, exposure times, atmospheres, or competing phase separation may change the predicted behavior.
